newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW--New CEO sees no mandate to change CBOE.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--New CEO sees no mandate to change CBOE.

text.p: William Brodsky, newly appointed chief executive officer of the Chicago Board Options Exchange, said Wednesday he did not have a mandate to change the largest options exchange in the U.S.

"I'm not going in with the idea that we have too much of this or too little of that," Brodsky said in a telephone interview. "I'm not going in there with an agenda to shake things up, but to provide a new outlook."
He said he had met with some CBOE board members "and I have a sense of what they think is working well."

Industry sources had said the choice to replace Alger "Duke" Chapman as the CBOE's chairman and CEO came down to Brodsky, president and CEO of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), and CBOE vice chairman William Floersch.

Before Wednesday's board meeting, some sources said Brodsky would get the post if the board felt the exchange needed shaking up, while Floersch would be the choice if it did not see the need for much change.
But Brodsky said he had no plans for big changes.
"I am not going to go in like a corporate raider and say we have to slash and burn this and that," he said.
"The CBOE is in incredibly good shape, both operationally and from the point of view of investor confidence," he said.
The CBOE has not set a date for Brodsky to assume his position and said only that he would take office "sometime after the first of the year."
When he does take office, Brodsky said, one of his first tasks will be to assess the CBOE's current situation and meet with staff, members and member firms.
"There are various constituents and I'll be meeting with all of them to get sense of what they like and what they'd like to see changed," he said.
He said he would also work to improve relations between the CBOE and the other U.S. options exchanges and to maintain the exchange's close relationship with the CME, where he has worked since 1982.

"A certain amount of friction is going to be natural among competitors, but there's a lot more in common than there is not in common," he said, stressing the fact that through his nearly 30 years in the financial industry he has maintained relationships with others in the business.
He said the CBOE's succession committee contacted him and that he had not been looking to leave the CME.
"I had been very happy at the Merc and I will keep my friends there," he said.
CME chairman Jack Sandner said in a statement the exchange would soon name a search committee to find Brodsky's replacement.
